facts.claim: Koren, Bell and Volinsky (IEEE Computer, 2009) write that, as the Netflix Prize showed, matrix factorization models beat classic nearest-neighbour methods at product recommendations.
The same article says factorization can also take in implicit feedback, changes over time and confidence levels.
Hu, Koren and Volinsky (ICDM 2008) treat implicit data, such as what people bought or watched, as signs of liking or not liking held with very different confidence.
Chaney, Stewart and Engelhardt (RecSys 2018) note that recommenders are trained on data from users already shown recommendations, a feedback loop.
In their simulations, that loop makes users’ behaviour more alike without making them better off.
Covington, Adams and Sargin (RecSys 2016) describe YouTube’s recommender in two stages: one model picks candidates from the catalogue, a second model ranks them.
